## What is the Tidyverse?

The **Tidyverse** is a collection of R packages designed for data science that share a common grammar, data structure, and design philosophy. All packages work with **tidy data**: one variable per column, one observation per row, one value per cell.

```{r tidyverse-logo, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%"}
# Core packages loaded by library(tidyverse):
# ggplot2   — data visualization
# dplyr     — data manipulation
# tidyr     — reshaping data
# readr     — importing rectangular data
# tibble    — modern data frames
# stringr   — string manipulation
# forcats   — categorical variables (factors)
# purrr     — functional programming
```

| Package  | Purpose                                               |
|----------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| ggplot2  | Data visualization                                    |
| dplyr    | Data manipulation (filter, select, mutate, summarise) |
| tidyr    | Reshaping data (pivot_longer, pivot_wider)            |
| readr    | Importing CSV, TSV, and delimited files               |
| tibble   | Modern data frames                                    |
| stringr  | String manipulation                                   |
| forcats  | Factor (categorical variable) handling                |
| purrr    | Functional programming                                |

```{webr-r}
# Install if needed (skip on OnDemand — already available)
# install.packages("tidyverse")
# install.packages("palmerpenguins")

library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

## Importing Data with readr (and readxl)

### CSV, TSV, and delimited files

readr functions all follow the same pattern: `read_*()`.

Useful `read_csv()` arguments:

```{r readr-args, eval=FALSE}
read_csv(
  "myfile.csv",
  col_types  = cols(SampleID = col_character(),
                    Reads_M  = col_double()),  # enforce types
  na         = c("", "NA", "N/A", "ND"),       # strings to treat as NA
  skip       = 2,                               # skip first 2 rows (e.g. merged headers)
  n_max      = 100,                             # read only first 100 rows (great for peeking)
  comment    = "#"                              # ignore lines starting with #
)
```

### Reading Excel files with readxl

readxl is not part of the core Tidyverse but is installed alongside it and is the standard way to read `.xlsx` and `.xls` files in R.

```{r readxl-demo, eval=FALSE}
library(readxl)

# Basic read — defaults to the first sheet
df <- read_xlsx("my_experiment.xlsx")

# Specify a sheet by name or index
df <- read_xlsx("my_experiment.xlsx", sheet = "Sample Info")
df <- read_xlsx("my_experiment.xlsx", sheet = 2)

# Skip merged header rows and set column names manually
df <- read_xlsx(
  "my_experiment.xlsx",
  sheet     = "counts",
  skip      = 3,
  col_names = c("gene", "A1", "A2", "B1", "B2")
)

# List all sheet names before reading
excel_sheets("my_experiment.xlsx")

# Read a specific cell range (useful for summary tables embedded in sheets)
df <- read_xlsx("my_experiment.xlsx", range = "B4:F20")
```

> **readxl vs openxlsx:** readxl is read-only but fast and dependency-free. Use openxlsx or writexl if you also need to write Excel files.

### Exporting data

```{r export, eval=FALSE}
# Write back to CSV (most portable)
write_csv(df, "cleaned_data.csv")

# Write compressed (adds .gz automatically)
write_csv(df, "cleaned_data.csv.gz")

# Write TSV
write_tsv(df, "cleaned_data.tsv")
```

## Meeting the Data

### Palmer Penguins

We use the **palmerpenguins** dataset throughout this workshop. It contains measurements for 344 penguins across 3 species from the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica.

```{webr-r}
# Print a preview
penguins

# One-line summary of columns, types, and first values
glimpse(penguins)
```

> `glimpse()` is your first move on any new dataset. It tells you: how many rows and columns, the data type of each column (`<fct>` = factor/categorical, `<dbl>` = decimal number, `<int>` = integer), and the first few values.

## Pipes: Reading Code Left to Right

Before learning the manipulation verbs, let's establish the syntax that connects them.

### Two styles, same result

```{webr-r}
# Nested style — read inside-out, count parentheses
arrange(
  select(
    filter(penguins, species == "Adelie"),
    species, bill_length_mm
  ),
  bill_length_mm
)
```

```{webr-r}
# Piped style — read left to right like a sentence
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie") |>
  select(species, bill_length_mm) |>
  arrange(bill_length_mm)
```

`|>` reads as "and then": *Take penguins, and then keep only Adelie, and then select two columns, and then sort by bill length.*

> **Keyboard shortcut:** Ctrl+Shift+M (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+Shift+M (Mac)  
> In RStudio: Tools → Global Options → Code → check "Use native pipe operator"

### Exercise 3A — Pipes

Using `penguins`, keep only rows where `island` is `"Biscoe"` and `flipper_length_mm` is not NA. Select just `species`, `island`, and `flipper_length_mm`. Use the pipe.

```{webr-r}
# YOUR TURN: Fill in the blanks
penguins |>
  filter(island == ___, !is.na(___)) |>
  select(___, ___, ___)
```

<details>
<summary>Solution</summary>

```r
penguins |>
  filter(island == "Biscoe", !is.na(flipper_length_mm)) |>
  select(species, island, flipper_length_mm)
```

</details>

## Data Wrangling with dplyr

The six verbs that cover ~80% of data manipulation tasks:

| Verb          | What it does                              |
|---------------|-------------------------------------------|
| `filter()`    | Keep rows that match a condition          |
| `select()`    | Keep only named columns                   |
| `mutate()`    | Add or modify a column                    |
| `arrange()`   | Sort rows by column values                |
| `group_by()`  | Split into invisible groups               |
| `summarise()` | Collapse groups to one summary row        |

### Building a pipeline — step by step

Type each step, run it, then add the next `|>`.

**Step 1: filter**

```{webr-r}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Chinstrap", !is.na(body_mass_g))
# Result: 68 rows
```

**Step 2: mutate**

```{webr-r}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Chinstrap", !is.na(body_mass_g)) |>
  mutate(mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000)
# Same 68 rows, new column mass_kg
```

**Step 3: select**

```{webr-r}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Chinstrap", !is.na(body_mass_g)) |>
  mutate(mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) |>
  select(species, sex, mass_kg)
```

**Step 4: group_by + summarise**

```{webr-r}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Chinstrap", !is.na(body_mass_g)) |>
  mutate(mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) |>
  select(species, sex, mass_kg) |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarise(
    n         = n(),
    mean_mass = mean(mass_kg),
    max_mass  = max(mass_kg)
  )
# Result: 2 rows (female / male)
```

**Step 5: arrange**

```{webr-r}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Chinstrap", !is.na(body_mass_g)) |>
  mutate(mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) |>
  select(species, sex, mass_kg) |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarise(
    n         = n(),
    mean_mass = mean(mass_kg),
    max_mass  = max(mass_kg)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_mass))
```

### Exercise 4A — Full pipeline

Starting from `penguins`, remove any row where `flipper_length_mm` or `bill_length_mm` is NA. Add a column `bill_to_flipper = bill_length_mm / flipper_length_mm`. Group by species, compute the mean and SD of `bill_to_flipper`. Arrange largest-to-smallest mean.

```{webr-r}
# YOUR TURN
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(___), !is.na(___)) |>
  mutate(___ = ___ / ___) |>
  group_by(___) |>
  summarise(
    mean_ratio = ___,
    sd_ratio   = ___
  ) |>
  arrange(___)
```

<details>
<summary>Solution</summary>

```r
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm), !is.na(bill_length_mm)) |>
  mutate(bill_to_flipper = bill_length_mm / flipper_length_mm) |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    mean_ratio = mean(bill_to_flipper),
    sd_ratio   = sd(bill_to_flipper)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_ratio))
```

Expected output:

```
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  species   mean_ratio sd_ratio
  <fct>          <dbl>    <dbl>
1 Chinstrap      0.459   0.0261
2 Adelie         0.407   0.0246
3 Gentoo         0.360   0.0188
```

</details>

### Useful commands

**Recoding values with `case_when()`**

```{webr-r}
penguins |>
  mutate(
    size_class = case_when(
      body_mass_g < 3500                          ~ "small",
      body_mass_g >= 3500 & body_mass_g < 4500   ~ "medium",
      body_mass_g >= 4500                         ~ "large",
      .default = NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  count(species, size_class)
```

**Applying a function to many columns with `across()`**

```{webr-r}
penguins |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 1))) |>
  glimpse()
```

**Renaming columns**

```{webr-r}
penguins |>
  rename(
    bill_len  = bill_length_mm,
    bill_dep  = bill_depth_mm,
    flipper   = flipper_length_mm,
    body_mass = body_mass_g
  ) |>
  names()
```

## Reshaping Data with tidyr

Most bioinformatics data starts in wide format (conditions as columns). Most tools and plots want long format (one observation per row).

### Wide → Long: `pivot_longer()`

```{webr-r}
counts_wide <- tribble(
  ~gene,    ~sample_A, ~sample_B, ~sample_C,
  "GAPDH",  1200,      980,       1050,
  "TP53",    340,      290,        410,
  "BRCA1",   55,       72,          61
)

counts_wide   # 3 rows, 4 columns
```

```{webr-r}
counts_long <- counts_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = starts_with("sample"),
    names_to  = "sample",
    values_to = "count"
  )

counts_long   # 9 rows, 3 columns
```

```{webr-r}
counts_long |>
  group_by(gene) |>
  summarise(
    mean_count = mean(count),
    sd         = sd(count)
  )
```

### Exercise 5A — pivot_longer

The dataframe below has one column per platform. Pivot it to long format so each row is one lab–platform combination with columns `lab`, `platform`, and `n_samples`.

```{webr-r}
lab_data <- tribble(
  ~lab,      ~Illumina, ~PacBio, ~Nanopore,
  "Lab A",   42,        8,       3,
  "Lab B",   18,        0,       15,
  "Lab C",   67,        12,      0
)

# YOUR TURN
lab_data |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = ___,
    names_to  = ___,
    values_to = ___
  )
```

<details>
<summary>Solution</summary>

```r
lab_data |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(Illumina, PacBio, Nanopore),
    names_to  = "platform",
    values_to = "n_samples"
  )
# Expected: 9 rows × 3 columns
```

</details>

### Long → Wide: `pivot_wider()`

```{webr-r}
counts_long |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = sample,
    values_from = count
  )
```

## Pair Coding Exercise

Work with a partner — one types, one navigates. Switch after 6 minutes.

Starting from the metadata CSV, produce a summary tibble with one row per sequencing platform showing:

- The number of samples
- The mean and maximum sequencing depth (in millions of reads)
- The total estimated cost (depth × $100 per million reads)

Export the result as `platform_summary.csv`.

```{webr-r}

# Download the metadata CSV from GitHub
file_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bioinformatics-workshop/Intro-to-Tidyverse-2025/refs/heads/main/data/metadata.csv"
download.file(file_url, "metadata.csv")

# Read the CSV
meta <- read_csv("metadata.csv")

# Rename columns for easier typing
meta <- meta |>
  rename(depth_M = `Sequencing Depth (M Reads)`, platform = `Sequencing Platform`)

glimpse(meta)  # check column names before writing the pipeline

# YOUR TURN
meta |>
  ___
```

<details>
<summary>Solution</summary>

```r
meta |>
  mutate(cost = depth_M * 100) |>
  group_by(platform) |>
  summarise(
    n_samples  = n(),
    mean_depth = mean(depth_M, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_depth  = max(depth_M,  na.rm = TRUE),
    total_cost = sum(cost,     na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n_samples)) |>
  write_csv("platform_summary.csv")
```

</details>

## Data Wrangling Challenges

Work solo. Start at Mild — move to Medium or Hot when ready.

### The dataset

```{webr-r}
sample_sheet <- tribble(
  ~SampleID, ~Treatment,  ~Replicate, ~RIN, ~Reads_M, ~Technician,  ~Platform,
  "S01",     "control",   1,          8.2,  42.1,     "jsmith",     "Illumina",
  "S02",     "control",   2,          7.9,  38.4,     "J. Smith",   "Illumina",
  "S03",     "treated",   1,          8.5,  51.2,     "jsmith",     "Illumina",
  "S04",     "treated",   2,          NA,   29.8,     "mlee",       "PacBio",
  "S05",     "treated",   3,          7.1,  35.0,     "M. Lee",     "PacBio",
  "S06",     "control",   3,          6.8,  44.7,     "mlee",       "Illumina"
)

sample_sheet
```

### MILD

1. Standardise technician names: all `jsmith`/`J. Smith` → `"J. Smith"`, all `mlee`/`M. Lee` → `"M. Lee"`.
2. Remove samples where RIN is NA.
3. Add a column `passes_qc` that is `TRUE` when `Reads_M >= 35`.

```{webr-r}
# YOUR TURN
clean <- sample_sheet |>
  mutate(
    Technician = case_when(
      Technician %in% c(___, ___) ~ "J. Smith",
      Technician %in% c(___, ___) ~ "M. Lee",
      .default = Technician
    )
  ) |>
  filter(___) |>
  mutate(passes_qc = ___)

clean
```

<details>
<summary>Core solution</summary>

```r
clean <- sample_sheet |>
  mutate(
    Technician = case_when(
      Technician %in% c("jsmith", "J. Smith") ~ "J. Smith",
      Technician %in% c("mlee",   "M. Lee")   ~ "M. Lee",
      .default = Technician
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(RIN)) |>
  mutate(passes_qc = Reads_M >= 35)

clean
# 5 rows (S04 removed), passes_qc column added
```

</details>

2. Group by `Technician` and `Platform`. Compute: number of samples, total reads, total cost.
3. Export as `tech_summary.csv`.

```{webr-r}
# YOUR TURN — start from clean
clean |>

    n_samples   = n(),
```

1. Pivot the Medium summary wide so each Platform is its own column of `total_cost`. Fill missing combinations with `0`.
2. Add a column `over_budget = TRUE` when total Illumina cost exceeds $4,000.

```{webr-r}
# YOUR TURN — build from the Stretch summary
clean |>
  mutate(cost = Reads_M * 100) |>
  group_by(Technician, Platform) |>
  summarise(total_cost = sum(cost), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = ___,
    values_from = ___,
    values_fill = ___
  ) |>
  mutate(over_budget = ___)
```

<details>
<summary>Challenge solution</summary>

```r
clean |>
  mutate(cost = Reads_M * 100) |>
  group_by(Technician, Platform) |>
  summarise(total_cost = sum(cost), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = Platform,
    values_from = total_cost,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  mutate(over_budget = Illumina > 4000)
```

### Additional Challenges

Using the messy data (metadata.csv) from the pair coding exercise, tidy up the dataset and address the following questions:

- [ ] Convert the column names to snake_case (e.g. Technician Name → technician_name, RNA Concentration ng/µL → rna_concentration_ng_ul)
- [ ] Count the NAs in each column and report the number of missing values per column
- [ ] Standardize technician_name so alice/Alice and BOB/Bob become Alice and Bob.
- [ ] Convert collection_temp ("25 C") to a numeric column collection_temp_c
- [ ] Split patient_treatment_batch (e.g. P107_Placebo_B2) into patient, arm and batch.
- [ ] Recode treatment_group so Low-Dose and High_Dose use the same separator style, and replace NA with "Unknown".
- [ ] Produce a table of the mean RNA concentration by technician_name and sequencer_platform.
- [ ] Flag invalid values: sequencing_depth_m has a negative value (RNA_S95). Flag impossible values rather than silently deleting them.
- [ ] Pivot the data to long format and generate ggplot2 visualizations of RNA concentration by technician_name and sequencer_platform.

## Tidy Data Checklist

**Is my data tidy?**

- [ ] Each variable is its own column
- [ ] Each observation is its own row
- [ ] Each value is in exactly one cell
- [ ] Column names are `snake_case`, not `Sample Name (ng/µL)`
- [ ] Dates are ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD), not 11/20/25
- [ ] No values encoded as cell colour or merged headers
- [ ] Numeric columns contain only numbers — not `>35` or `ND`
